questions.prompt: Under what condition can WDigest cache plaintext-recoverable credentials in LSASS memory?
options: This happens by default on all current Windows versions
Only if the UseLogonCredential registry value has been set to re-enable it, since Microsoft disabled this caching by default starting with Windows 8.1/Server 2012 R2
WDigest never caches any credential material under any circumstances
Only on Windows Server, never on workstations
questions.explanation: WDigest plaintext credential caching was disabled by default starting with Windows 8.1/Server 2012 R2, but can be re-enabled via the UseLogonCredential registry key -- checking whether it's been re-enabled is a worthwhile investigative step.

questions.prompt: Why is "LSASS was accessed" the wrong question to ask when investigating potential credential theft?
options: LSASS should never be accessed by any process under any circumstances

LSASS is accessed constantly by ordinary system components as part of normal operation -- the kind of access requested, not whether access happened, is what actually distinguishes theft from routine activity
LSASS access cannot be logged in any way
Only Sysmon can detect LSASS access, no other tool can
questions.explanation: Treating any LSASS access as suspicious produces overwhelming noise, since routine system processes access it constantly. The GrantedAccess rights requested is what separates a credential-dumping attempt from background activity.

questions.prompt: What does LSA Protection (RunAsPPL) specifically prevent?
options: It prevents any process from ever running on the system
It makes LSASS a Protected Process Light, so ordinary usermode code -- even running as SYSTEM -- cannot open a full-access handle to it without a signed, Microsoft-trusted driver
It encrypts all files on the system
It disables the WDigest protocol entirely
questions.explanation: RunAsPPL elevates LSASS to a Protected Process Light, blocking ordinary usermode access regardless of privilege level -- which is exactly why attackers turn to BYOVD (a signed but vulnerable driver) to work around it.

questions.prompt: Why is checking for an existing LSASS dump file on disk often more directly actionable than live memory analysis?
options: Dump files never actually contain useful evidence
A dump file is the finished product of a successful (or attempted) dumping tool run, making it a direct artifact rather than something requiring live memory analysis to confirm
LSASS memory can never be analyzed after the fact
Dump files are automatically deleted by Windows within seconds
questions.explanation: A dump file left behind by a tool like ProcDump or comsvcs.dll's MiniDump is direct, concrete evidence of an attempt -- often faster to find and more conclusive than reconstructing the same conclusion from live memory analysis.
